newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tourism shrinks Japan current account surplus.
newsitem.headline: Tourism shrinks Japan current account surplus.

text.p: Japan's current account surplus dropped a solid 15 percent in November from a year earlier, pushed down by surge in spending by Japanese tourists abroad.

The Finance Ministry said on Monday that the surplus in the current account -- the broadest measure of trade in goods and services -- fell 15.4 percent in November from a year earlier to 664 billion yen ($5.72 billion).
However economists said it would be only a matter of time before the weaker yen pushed the surplus higher again.

The trade surplus in goods stayed virtually level in November compared with a year ago, slipping a mere three percent, but a rise in the number of Japanese travelling abroad helped the deficit in services widen by 27 percent.

Japanese people's love affair with foreign climes saw overseas spending for November at its highest level in five years, resulting in a travel deficit growth of 15 billion yen ($129 million) to 293 billion yen ($2.52 billion) from a year earlier.

The current account surplus has been declining steadily since late 1994, helped by a strong yen, which made exports less competitively priced in overseas markets and encouraged domestic manufacturers to shift factories to cheaper bases abroad.
But the 15 percent drop was larger than economists had expected. They had predicted an average fall of around six percent.
The economists had expected the pace of decline in the surplus to slow dramatically from previous months as the weakening of the yen over the past year boosted exports.
"Obviously, this process of trade adjustment is taking longer than expected," said Matthew Poggi, an economist at Lehman Brothers.
But economists also said the surplus in the current account was likely to rise again in 1997, with some predicting the first increases in the first quarter.
"I think that in the next three to five months, we are going to see gradually the trade surplus starting to move higher," said Jesper Koll, head of research at J.P. Morgan.
"When you look at the overall momentum provided by currency depreciation you do in fact find that Japan's manufacturers are benefiting," he said.
Imports of oil are also expected to fall back once winter is over, helping to push the surplus higher, economists said.

Currency dealers in particular are wary of renewed increases in the surplus -- often a cause of trade friction between Japan and its largest trading partner, the United States. "It could become a problem at that time, at which point we will need to watch for the U.S. response," said Nobuo Kihara, a corporate dealer at Banque Paribas.
The dollar has risen sharply since hitting a post-war low of 79.75 yen in April 1995. It was trading at around 116 yen on Monday.
